name: NATIONAL ACADEMY OF SCIENCES
agency: Department of Health and Human Services
naics_description: OTHER SCIENTIFIC AND TECHNICAL CONSULTING SERVICES
brief_text:
Four detectors flagged National Academy of Sciences. Benford's law analysis found the leading-digit distribution of award amounts significantly deviates from expected frequencies, with an unusually high proportion of awards starting with 1 or 2. Modification growth on one contract grew 178-fold, far exceeding the typical 13-fold ratio for peers in scientific consulting. The entity also emerged as a multivariate outlier, combining high dollar volume, concentrated agency relationships, and frequent contract modifications. Finally, sole-source awards comprise 93 percent of its portfolio versus a median of 1.4 percent for comparable firms.

The Benford test yielded a p-value of 0.00007 across 248 transactions. The worst-performing contract (HHSD200201138807I) showed a growth ratio of 178.51 against a NAICS average of 13.25, producing a z-score of 3.60. Sole-source awards totaled 230 of 248 (92.7 percent), with a z-score of 2.53 relative to peer standard deviation. The isolation forest assigned an anomaly score of 0.86, reflecting the entity's extreme position on multiple dimensions simultaneously.

National Academy of Sciences is a congressionally chartered nonprofit with a legitimate federal advisory mission, which contextualizes some signals. High sole-source concentration and modification frequency align with its role providing specialized scientific expertise and policy analysis. However, the Benford deviation and extreme modification growth on a single contract warrant scrutiny. The peer group for scientific consulting is small and heterogeneous, limiting statistical power. The combination of signals—particularly the 178-fold modification ratio—merits closer examination of contract justifications and pricing practices.
